unit.title: Do the stories we watch change us?
unit.needIt: Shows, games and feeds work on the part of you that does not argue back. Knowing that, you can choose what you and your children soak in.
unit.why: Plato argued that stories affect the parts of our soul that do not use logic. He believed that if we watch heroes do bad things, we might start to think those actions are okay. This is why he thought the government should choose which stories people are allowed to see.
unit.outcome: Recognize how fictional stories shape your habits and emotions.
unit.reachesYou: You see this when you watch a show and find yourself liking a character's bad choices. You also feel it when a video game makes a violent action feel like a natural instinct.
unit.do: Think about a show you enjoy and ask yourself if the characters' actions are things you would actually want to do in real life.

quiz.q: What is the main problem with the prisoner's dilemma?
choices: It is a paradox of rationality
quiz.why: The lecture describes the prisoner's dilemma as a paradox of rationality where self-interests conflict.
quiz.quote: The argument that Hobbes makes appeals to the notion of the prisoner's dilemma, which is a paradox of rationality.

quiz.q: What did Dan Quayle say about Murphy Brown?
quiz.why: Quayle argued that her character's choices were a moral issue requiring social sanction.
quiz.quote: And the then Vice President of the United States, Dan Quayle, famously gave a speech in San Francisco in 1992 at which he he said, marriage is a moral issue that requires consensus

quiz.q: Why did Dan Quayle criticize the show Murphy Brown?
quiz.why: He believed the show eroded values that are important to the country.
quiz.quote: Dan Quayle slightly misrepresented what happened on the show. Murphy Brown, though she lacked a long-term partner and did bear a child without the support of a second adult figure, didn't call it just a lifestyle choice.

quiz.q: How do people react to the show 24?
choices: They saw it as a role model
quiz.why: The lecture explains that the show provided conceptual space for people to see different types of leaders.
quiz.quote: What it points out is that the availability in fictional representation of a character who served as president and was of African descent, or who served as president and was a played some role in allowing actual citizens in the real world, not imaginary people on TV, to have conceptual space available for the possibility of there being a president of that kind.

quiz.why: The puzzle is how something we know is fictional can still change our actual attitudes.
quiz.quote: Now, the puzzle that this raises, if we think only in terms of rationality, is the following. How can something that we know to be fictional affect our actual behaviors and attitudes.

quiz.q: What is the 'puzzle' regarding fiction and behavior?
quiz.why: The puzzle is how something we know is fake can still change our real attitudes.
quiz.quote: How can something that we know to be fictional affect our actual behaviors and attitudes.

quiz.q: What does Plato say about the 'imitative poet'?
choices: He appeals to an inferior part
quiz.why: Plato argues that the poet appeals to the part of the soul that is not rational.
quiz.quote: He says, the imitative poet appeals to a part of the soul that is inferior.

partials: Fiction affects non-rational parts of the soul.
Reason alone cannot regulate these effects.
Stories can provide problematic role models.
Habits are formed through early imitation.
External regulation may be necessary for harmony.
crystal.key: Fiction can shape our non-rational habits in ways that reason alone cannot control.

decoys.text: People are always aware of the difference between fiction and reality.
decoys.why: The lecture says that even if we are aware, the non-rational parts of the soul can still be affected.

decoys.text: All forms of imitation are dangerous to the soul.
decoys.why: Plato distinguishes between 'playful imitation' and the more problematic types of imitation.

crystal.aha: Because our souls have non-rational parts, stories can shape our habits even when we know they are fake, requiring external rules to maintain harmony.

scene.analogy: A song stuck in your head

beats.say: You hear a catchy song once.
You did not decide to remember it.
All day it plays in your head.
Stories build habits, so Plato wanted them chosen with care.
